Landed. torcl f373a73e (the gate, runtime API 3) and bliss 2a4b171 (EditText through it).

Verified on a Pixel 10 Pro XL, Android 16: mServedInputConnection is an

Two things learned that were not in the plan:

* A jobject returned from a main-thread visit is a LOCAL reference belonging to
  MessageQueue.nativePollOnce's JNI frame, and that frame is popped when the
  looper returns to Java. Promoting it on the next visit aborts the process
  (CheckJNI: 'invalid local reference, popped reference at index 11 in a table
  of size 7'). The gate therefore takes optional promote/release functions,
  supplied by the caller, applied before the visit ends.
* Java strings are MODIFIED UTF-8, and neither direction was handling it. Now
  in bliss src/utf8.lisp with 9 desktop checks.

8d60e57. WITH-LOCAL-REFS (PushLocalFrame/PopLocalFrame) now wraps every per-frame and per-keystroke JNI path.

IMPORTANT CORRECTION to this bead's own premise. It claimed leaked local refs
'overflow the table and abort'. Measured on a Pixel 10 Pro XL, Android 16, that
is false: 1,000 / 50,000 / 250,000 unframed object-returning calls all survived
with the process healthy. 512 is the minimum the JNI SPEC obliges an
implementation to guarantee, not ART's limit -- ART grows the table.

What it does cost, also measured: 200,000 leaked references moved the process
from 118,957 KB PSS to 128,052 KB. About 45 bytes each, plus each one pins the
Java object it names.

So: real leak, right fix, wrong severity. Unbounded growth and uncollectable
objects, not a crash.

Verified on the desktop: 7 checks, including that a damaged redraw is
pixel-identical to a full one. Kept, because the software rasterizer's cost IS
per-pixel and it genuinely helps there.

On the phone it is flat, across three measurements:

  dragging the carousel   damage  8-18%   present ~32ms   (unclipped 28-42ms)
  typing in a text field  damage 12-23%   present ~33ms
  CLIPPED TO ONE PIXEL    damage      0   present 30-45ms

That last one is the answer. Drawing NOTHING costs the same as drawing
everything, so present's cost is not the drawing. It is issuing ~100 operations
through JNI -- each of which is three to six calls at ~35us plus argument
marshalling -- and a clip removes none of that.

Note the apparent contradiction with the earlier measurement that turning
shadows OFF took present from 42ms to 20-34ms. Both are true: the blur is
genuinely expensive AND the clip does not avoid it, which says Skia computes a
BlurMaskFilter's mask before the clip rejects it. Removing the op helps; clipping
it does not.

So present is bounded by the NUMBER of operations and by blur, not by area.
Follow-ups: bliss-<batching> and caching a blurred shadow as a bitmap.

Found a latent bug in WITH-LOCAL-REFS on the way: it kept only the primary value, so (VALUES 0 0 0 0) arrived as 0 and three NILs.

Fixed in TorCL, not in Bliss. Root cause: the tree-walking MULTIPLE-VALUE-PROG1 held its TRAILING forms in an unrooted Rust local across the evaluation of its first form -- which, in BLISS:WITH-FRAME-CLOCK, is an entire UI frame. A minor GC relocated the body and the cursor was left pointing at an address; a JNI argument list was allocated there, so the cleanup form became a list of four foreign pointers and the evaluator reported 'The function #<heap-object type=27> is undefined'. Tracked as torcl bliss-ro3an, fixed with a regression test.

A :PLATFORM-VIEW node lays out like a box and paints nothing; PLATFORM-VIEW-RECTS reports its window pixels; the Android half attaches a real View. 11 new tests, 388 checks, 0 failures. The Android half is pure JNI with no desktop equivalent and is claimed only on what was seen on the phone.

SEEN WORKING: a WebView with inline HTML -- bold, italic, a bulleted list -- between the shelf and the Name field, tracking the page scroll exactly through several drags and a light/dark switch.

THE BEAD'S PREMISE WAS BACKWARDS and it cost the first attempt. It predicted a child View would draw ABOVE our surface. With addContentView the opposite happens: a NativeActivity's ANativeWindow and the Java view hierarchy are the SAME surface (dumpsys SurfaceFlinger lists one buffer layer, VRI-org.bliss.demo), so both draw into one buffer and whoever posts last wins -- and we post a whole frame whenever anything changes. The first WebView was attached and laid out at exactly the right bounds per uiautomator dump ([34,1698][1046,2058]) and completely invisible.

The fix is WindowManager.addView with TYPE_APPLICATION_PANEL, which gives the View its own SurfaceFlinger layer above ours. That INVERTS the z-order problem rather than solving it: the embedded View is now always on top. Visible in the demo -- open the dialog and the scrim dims everything Bliss drew while the WebView stays bright above it.

Clipping is still unsolved and cannot be solved this way: a View whose rectangle has left the viewport entirely is hidden (desktop-tested), partial overlap still bleeds. Filed nothing for it yet; a SurfaceView with Z-ordering is the platform answer and needs a Java class.

Committed as 55d16a3 (demo 69b1a85). :CLIP-PUSH carries a RADIUS; the clip stack becomes (AREA RADIUS ROUND) and CLIP-SPANS yields one span for a square clip and one per row for a rounded one. Canvas uses Skia clipPath with a single reused Path; the rectangle-only backends get it through FLATTEN-TO-RECTS. 14 new tests, 402 checks, 0 failures.

The bead's diagnosis was right, which is worth recording after five that were not. One thing it did not mention and that mattered: DRAW-IMAGE does not go through FILL-CLIPPED, so an image kept square corners even where everything else was cut -- and the image demo it cited is exactly that path.

Simplification, documented in the code: two nested ROUNDED clips keep the inner radius only.

SEEN ON THE PHONE: two full-bleed stripes inside a :RADIUS 24 container, all four corners rounded and crisp at pixel zoom, in dark and in light.
